title: 10 things UBC students should know about academic integrity
content_markdown:
[Web banner for 10 things UBC students should know about academic integrity](https://academic.ubc.ca/sites/default/files/inline-images/Integrity_Web.png)

#### [Download the *10 things\.\.\.* as PDF](https://academic.ubc.ca/sites/default/files/2025-09/UBC-10-Things-Integrity.pdf)

### 1\. Not all uses of GenAI are academic misconduct, but some may be\.

Generative AI tools are becoming more powerful and are often integrated into other applications you may already use \(Grammarly, Microsoft 365, etc\.\)\. You will encounter different rules for GenAI use in each of your courses, as faculty members design their individual courses and assessments\. Some classes might allow it for brainstorming, others might not permit use for assessed work\. When in doubt, check your course syllabus or ask your instructor directly\. Learning at the university level can – and should – be challenging\. Using AI responsibly means using it to support and augment your learning, not to do the work for you\.

*Resource links:*

-   [10 things UBC students should know about GenAI](https://academic.ubc.ca/teaching-learning/10-things-ubc-students-should-know/generative-ai "10 things UBC students should know about generative AI")
-   [Learning with GenAI Student Guidelines](https://genai.ubc.ca/guidance/teaching-learning-guidelines/learning-with-genai/)

### 2\. Not all misconduct will get you suspended, but it is a possibility\.

Academic misconduct can have serious consequences, including suspension\. The Dean’s Office will decide whether to resolve the misconduct through a Warning Letter, the Diversionary Process, or the President’s Advisory Committee on Student Discipline \(PACSD\)\. Suspension is a potential outcome for PACSD cases\. It is important to take every allegation seriously and seek support early\.

*Resource links:*

-   [Annual Summaries of Student Discipline](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/homepage/guides-and-resources/discipline/annual-summaries/)
-   [Academic misconduct process for students](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students/)

### 3\. Tutors can be a valuable learning support but be wary when their services seem too good to be true\.

Tutors can help you better understand course concepts but should not do your work for you\. Be wary of tutors who promise a guaranteed grade, provide solutions or edits to your assignments, or ask for your CWL login\. UBC offers ethical options including peer academic coaching, research support, and writing consultations\. A good tutor helps you understand course material and improves your academic skills but does not do your assessed work\.

*Resource links:*

-   Vancouver:
    -   [Chapman Learning Commons](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/)
    -   [Tutoring and Coaching \- Learning Commons](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/tutoring-and-coaching/)
    -   [Centre for Writing and Scholarly Communication](https://writing.library.ubc.ca/)
-   Okanagan:
    -   [Student Learning Hub](https://students.ok.ubc.ca/academic-success/learning-hub/)
    -   [Okanagan Library](https://library.ok.ubc.ca/research/)
    -   [Centre for Scholarly Communication](https://csc.ok.ubc.ca/)

### 4\. Don’t be tempted by sites and services that promise answers, shortcuts, and easy ways out\.

You might encounter ads or messages promising access to course materials, assignment help and better grades\. Some might even offer exam solutions or essay\-writing services\. It is cheating to get someone else to do your work for you, paid or not\. Some of these services can be predatory and might threaten to report their users to the institution, impersonate students, or even blackmail them\. Exercise caution with “study\-help” services and do not share your CWL with anyone\.

*Resource link:*

-   [Contract cheating – UBC Academic Integrity website](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/teaching-and-learning/contract-cheating/)

### 5\. Sharing your work or course materials can be misconduct, and it can also infringe copyright rules\.

Think carefully before sharing your work or your course materials with other people or online \(such as in group chats or posting on file\-sharing sites\)\. Sharing your work carries considerable risk\. For instance, it might get plagiarized by someone else, or you might be providing unauthorized assistance to other students\. Course materials provided to you \(like lecture slides, assessments, and syllabi\) are the intellectual property of the instructor\(s\) who created them\. Sharing them without permission can violate copyright laws\.

*Resource link:*

-   [Copyright at UBC](https://copyright.ubc.ca/copyright-guidelines/)

### 6\. Working with others is an important skill: it’s \(usually\) OK to give and receive help from your peers, but how you do it matters\.

Collaboration is a big part of learning and an important skill\. However, not all collaboration is allowed\. What is allowed in one course or assignment might be misconduct in another\. Studying with a classmate is often encouraged, as long as you are not copying or helping each other complete individually assessed work\. Unauthorized collaboration, whether in group work or while working on assignments, may be considered academic misconduct\. When in doubt, ask your instructor what type of collaboration is acceptable\.

*Resource links:*

-   [Collaborative Learning and Group Work – UBC Academic Integrity website](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/teaching-and-learning/collaborative-learning/)

### 7\. Make sure you understand what 'open book’ means and what you can and cannot bring to your exams\.

Make sure to follow all exam or test instructions from your professor and invigilator, including any rules about what material or devices you can bring or use\. Keep anything that is not permitted \(phone, notes, textbook etc\.\) stored away and off your person\. Do not use your phone as a calculator \- using or being in possession of an unauthorized resource during an exam can be considered academic misconduct\. And remember, an “open book” exam may not mean you can use any or every tool you want\. If you need clarity around what “open book” means for your assessment, ask your instructor for more information\.

*Resource links*: 

-   Student Conduct during Examinations, UBC Academic Calendar \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/academic-assessment/student-conduct-during-examinations)/[Okanagan\)](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/academic-assessment/examinations/student-conduct-during-examinations)

### 8\. Not knowing is not an excuse\.

As a UBC student, you are expected to understand and follow the rules about academic integrity\. Read your course syllabus, assignment instructions, and UBC’s academic integrity policy\. If something is unclear \(like whether you can use AI, work with a friend, or reuse your own past work\), ask your instructor or TA before you act\. Being informed is not just about avoiding trouble: it is your responsibility\.

*Resource links:*

-   Expectations of Academic Integrity, Discipline for Academic Misconduct, UBC Academic Calendar \([Vancouver](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/teaching-and-learning/collaborative-learning/)/[Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/1-expectations-academic-integrity)\)

### 9\. Resources are available to support you in learning with integrity\.

If you are struggling in your courses, reach out for help\. UBC has academic and wellbeing supports to help you stay on track\. Your instructor is also here to help and can direct you to other supports that are available\. Using these supports is not a sign of weakness; it is a smart way to build your skills and confidence and shows that you take academic integrity seriously\.

*Resource links:*

-   Vancouver:
    -   [Academic Integrity Hub](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/aihub/)
    -   [Academic and Learning Resources](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/academic-learning-resources/)
    -   [Student Health and Wellbeing](http://students.ubc.ca/health/)
-   Okanagan:
    -   [Academic Integrity Matters \(AIM\) Program](https://students.ok.ubc.ca/academic-success/learning-hub/faculty-resources/academic-integrity/)
    -   [Learning Strategists](https://students.ok.ubc.ca/academic-success/learning-hub/learning-strategist/)
    -   [Student Wellness](https://students.ok.ubc.ca/health-wellness/)

### 10\. If an allegation of academic misconduct is made against you, here’s what you can do\.

Being accused of academic misconduct can feel overwhelming\. You may be concerned about impacts on your studies, degree progression, and your wellbeing\. Take some time to learn about your options, the process, and where to get support\. You must be given an opportunity to respond to the allegation before the Dean’s Office makes their decision\. If you have concerns about the fairness of the misconduct process, false accusations, or would like some additional support, reach out early to the Ombudsperson for Students or advocacy services\. You do not have to go through the process alone\.

*Resource links:*

-   [Ombudsperson for Students](https://ombudsoffice.ubc.ca/)
-   [AMS Advocacy](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-services/advocacy/)
-   [GSS Peer Support](https://gss.ubc.ca/peer-support/)
-   [SUO Advocates](https://www.suo.ca/suo-advocacy-office/)
-   [Human Rights Advising](https://equity.ubc.ca/how-we-can-help/human-rights-advising/)

This resource was created in July 2025 under the direction of the Academic Integrity Hub\. This is an educative resource intended to support understanding of the topics and associated processes and does not constitute legal advice nor impose legal obligations on the University\. The content of this resource may be updated\. The Academic Calendar is the official governing document, and where there is any inconsistency or contradiction between this educative resource and the Academic Calendar provisions governing academic integrity and academic misconduct, the Academic Calendar governs\. This resource was created with the assistance of GenAI tools\. It was reworked and revised by humans\.

# BC Academic Integrity Day

### October 13, 2023

[Announcement icon](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2022/07/awareness-on-white.png)

Hosted this year by the University of British Columbia, BC Academic Integrity Day is a forum to connect, learn and share resources to inspire best practices in academic integrity and to advance scholarship and professionalism\. We invite students, faculty, and practitioners from across higher education institutions in BC and beyond to attend and participate in the discussion\. The day will feature a networking lunch and resource sharing opportunities\.

The full program and session descriptions from the event can be [downloaded here](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/files/2023/10/BCAI-Day-2023-Program-and-Session-Descriptions.pdf)\.

title: Editorial: The evolution of generative AI in teaching and learning at UBC
content_markdown:
[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/04/May-2024-editorial.jpg)

*Written by [Christina Hendricks,](https://academic.ubc.ca/about-vp-academic/profile/christina-hendricks) Vice\-Provost and Associate Vice\-President, Teaching and Learning* pro tem*, UBC Vancouver; [Tamara Ebl](https://management.ok.ubc.ca/about/contact/tamara-ebl/), Lecturer, Faculty of Management, UBC Okanagan, and UBC Okanagan Teaching Fellow 2023\-2024; and [Kamil Kanji](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/about-us/leadership/), Elected Student Senator\-at\-Large, Vice Chair of the UBC Vancouver Senate, Vice Chair of the UBCV Senate Academic Policy Committee and elected Vice President of the Student Legal Fund Society\.*

---

In the fall of 2023, UBC created the [Generative AI in Teaching and Learning Advisory Committee](https://genai.ubc.ca/committee/subcommittees/teaching-and-learning-advisory/), with a wide membership across both campuses, and the three of us as co\-chairs\. Given questions and concerns about generative AI \(GenAI\) and academic integrity within UBC community, academic integrity quickly became one of the prominent discussion topics in the group, though many others have emerged as well\.

This Advisory Committee is one of several subcommittees of the broader [UBC Generative AI Steering Committee](https://genai.ubc.ca/committee/) that was established in spring 2023 with a wide remit, including discussion of opportunities and risks of GenAI in teaching and learning, administrative activities, communications, technology development and support, and more\.

The Advisory Committee focuses on benefits, challenges, and risks of using GenAI tools in teaching and learning activities, including in the areas of academic integrity, Indigenous data sovereignty, equity and inclusivity, accessibility, privacy, and intellectual property\. The Advisory Committee has met monthly since October 2023 and will continue until June 2024\.

One of the Advisory Committee’s main objectives has been to develop a set of principles and guidelines for students, faculty, teaching assistants and staff use of GenAI tools in teaching and learning\. These guidelines are meant to provide more specific direction within a broader set of principles on GenAI produced through the UBC Generative AI Steering Committee\. You can find them here: [Principles for the Use of Generative AI Tools](https://it-genai-2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/04/Principles-for-the-use-of-Generative-AI.pdf)\.

Having people with multiple experiences, expertise, and perspectives involved in generating and refining such principles and guidelines has been a key driver for the membership from both campuses, which includes faculty and students, along with representatives from Graduate Studies, VP Students offices, the UBC Library, the Ombudsperson for students, the Centre for Teaching & Learning \(UBCO\) & Centre for Teaching, Learning & Technology \(UBCV\), and the Academic Integrity Hub \(UBCV\)\.

### Co\-Chair perspectives

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/04/Christina-Hendricks-genAI.jpg)

As a Professor of Teaching in Philosophy and Vice\-Provost and Associate Vice\-President Teaching and Learning *pro tem*, **Christina Hendricks** wants to ensure that many people with various experiences, expertise, and roles are involved in developing institutional principles and guidelines for GenAI in teaching and learning\. It has been crucial to have students, faculty, and staff from many different disciplines, units, and portfolios involved in discussions, including advice on communications, resources, and events to support further learning about GenAI amongst the UBC community\.

\.

---

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/04/Tamara-Ebl.jpg)

As a contract Lecturer with over a decade of experience teaching on UBC’s Okanagan campus, **Tamara Ebl** appreciates the complex challenges faced by students, faculties, TAs, and staff throughout the UBC community, particularly with respect to the relatively recent introduction and rapid pace of advancement of ChatGPT \(and other similar GenAI technologies\)\. Tamara’s perspective continues to evolve, but it remains her focus to promote timely development and clear communication of relevant principles and guidelines to thoughtfully address the challenges and promote practical opportunities for use of GenAI in constructive ways\.

\.\.

---

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/04/Kamil-Kanji.jpg)

As a UBC Vancouver Student Senator and also the Vice\-President Academic Affairs of the Alma Mater Society, **Kamil Kanji** emphasizes the importance of having student leadership from both campuses on the committee, to better consider the various needs of students as well as faculty and staff\. It has been an excellent mapping experience to really consider the impact GenAI is having on students and how we can utilize it in a way that is less punitive but far more constructive towards achieving learning objectives\. By centering students in this process we divert from inherent teaching biases that may jump to the total exclusion of GenAI use in classrooms to solutions that are more focused on integration into pedagogical approaches\.

\.\.

---

### Upcoming guidelines on GenAI in Teaching and Learning

For the last few months, the Generative AI in Teaching and Learning Advisory Committee has been actively working on a set of principles and guidelines for using GenAI in teaching and learning by students, faculty, TAs, and staff\. The principles and guidelines are currently in draft form and undergoing consultations  across the university\. The draft guidelines have a set of broad principles that act as a foundation, focusing on respecting Indigenous data sovereignty rights; supporting equity and inclusion; upholding academic integrity, privacy and confidentiality; respecting copyright and intellectual property; disclosing and attributing use of GenAI; and ensuring human oversight of AI\-generated work used for teaching and learning\. In addition, the guidelines provide specific guidance to instructors and TAs about teaching with GenAI, and to students about learning with GenAI\.

Academic integrity features prominently throughout the document, being highlighted in providing guidance for instructors on communicating with students if and how they are permitted to use GenAI tools for their coursework, advice about the use of AI detector tools, and guidance for instructors and students about disclosing and attributing use of GenAI in their academic work\.

Advisory Committee discussions about these principles and guidelines have been rich and have revealed numerous complexities, including that the types and capabilities of such tools continue to change even as we are discussing how to use and adapt to them\. Accordingly, even after consulting with many more partners in the institution we know we will not get everything right, and that these principles and guidelines will need to adapt over time\. The Advisory Committee aims to share the first version with the UBC community in the next few months, and will also be considering a process for further iteration over time\. Please refer to the [Advisory Committee website](https://genai.ubc.ca/committee/subcommittees/teaching-and-learning-advisory/) further for further information\.

title: Academic Integrity Digest: September 2024
content_markdown:
[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/09/AID-Hero-Sept-2024-2.jpg)

Welcome to the Fall edition of the Academic Integrity Digest, and welcome back to campus for the 2024/25 academic year\.

This issue’s theme continues to explore the intersection of academic integrity and generative AI\. Specifically, the editorial takes a deeper look into tools for detecting the use of artificial intelligence and presents research on their efficacy, suitability and performance in detecting academic misconduct\. In the resource section, you will find updated information to support and guide decisions around the use of generative AI in teaching and learning\. UBC will mark Academic Integrity Week October 15\-18 with a variety of events and engagement sessions on each campus\. See the events section for more details\.

---

#### *Editorial*

## **The flawed promise of generative AI writing detectors**

**Dr\. Simon Bates, Vice\-Provost and Associate Vice\-President, Teaching and Learning \(UBCV\)  
Heather Berringer, Associate Provost, Academic Operations and Services \(UBCO\)**

Early reactions to widespread availability of generative AI writing tools such as ChatGPT included concerns over a low barrier route to misconduct in unsupervised assessments\. “The College Essay Is Dead”, cried the headlines in the popular press [**\[1\]**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/2024/09/19/academic-integrity-digest-september-2024/#_ftn1)\. Initial institutional and individual responses were mixed: some saw it as a golden opportunity to rethink and retool assessments to focus on process and not just on the final product\. This, argued those with that perspective, was essential for a degree to stay relevant in an era when AI would soon be built directly into widely available suites of digital tools\. The inverse reaction was to seek technology as impressive as the generative tools themselves to reliably and accurately detect AI\-generated passages of text\. Proponents of this approach argued it was essential to remain one step ahead of those looking to pass AI\-generated text off as their own\.

AI\-generation detectors sprang up with bold claims about efficacy and utility, but no transparency about how they were trained, what dataset was used to evaluate them, or any ability to reproduce the results\. These detection tools and the methods of use that wrap around them provided no student visibility into how their writing was being evaluated, and led UBC to not enable Turnitin’s AI\-detection feature in April 2023 [**\[2\]**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/2024/09/19/academic-integrity-digest-september-2024/#_ftn2), a decision re\-affirmed in August 2023 [**\[3\]**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/2024/09/19/academic-integrity-digest-september-2024/#_ftn3)\. A year later, even more detector tools are available; in what follows, we summarize some recently\-published research that illustrates how these tools perform under a systematic battery of tests that include human\-generated, AI\-generated, translated, and obfuscated texts\.

Weber\-Wulff *et al* [**\[4\]**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/2024/09/19/academic-integrity-digest-september-2024/#_ftn4) published a comprehensive study of 14 available tools each given five test cases of pre\-written text of between 2000 and 10,000 characters\. More detail follows, but:

1.  All AI\-generated text detection tools evaluated have serious limitations, contrary to claims made by their developers / vendors\.
2.  They too often present significant instances of false positives and false negatives, both of which carry serious repercussions for students\.
3.  No tool accurately predicts the authorship of a text better than 80%; many struggle to reach 70%\.
4.  It is easy to obfuscate systems with translation, text manipulation and paraphrasing and further reduce accuracy of prediction of all tools\. 

One of the research challenges was mapping the various outputs to a consistent scale that could be used to compare across tools\. Some tools output a percentage likelihood of human / AI authorship, while others use statements like “possibly AI generated\.” To compare performance of different tools, researchers mapped outputs onto a five\-point scale of assessment used as a basis for classification of accuracy and error type\. As an example, text written by an AI tool in the test dataset should be detected as a ‘positive’ result if the detection tool is effective; in this case the actual performance of the detection tool is classified as one of 5 options: True Positive, Partially True Positive, Unclear, Partially False Negative, False Negative\. Detection tools are evaluated as to their accuracy \(by tool and by document type\) and the rate at which they produce false positive \(text is human\-written but flagged as AI\-written\) and false negative \(text is AI written but flagged as human written\) errors\. The figure below from the paper illustrates overall accuracy for each tool calculated as an average of all approaches discussed\. It illustrates the third conclusion noted above: no tool performs with higher than 80% accuracy, with most well below that\.

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/09/newsletter-graph-image-2.jpg)

Widespread availability of generative AI tools presents real challenges to assessment design, but a quick fix detection tool is not the answer\. They are not sufficiently accurate, the methodology of how they arrive at a conclusion is opaque, and they are too easily gamed by simple obfuscation techniques\. Efforts should instead focus on preventative and educative approaches, including a rethink of assessment strategies and activities, and a renewed focus on evidencing the process of learning rather than simply assessing a final product\. This is most certainly non\-trivial and looks very different in different disciplinary contexts, but it is vitally important as we continue to build and maintain a culture of integrity at UBC\.

---

\[1\] Quite literally, that was the title\. “The College Essay is Dead” The Atlantic, December 2012 [https://www\.theatlantic\.com/technology/archive/2022/12/chatgpt\-ai\-writing\-college\-student\-essays/672371/](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2022/12/chatgpt-ai-writing-college-student-essays/672371/) \(retrieved July 30\[th\] 2024\)\.

\[2\] “UBC not enabling Turnitin’s AI detection feature” April 2023 [https://lthub\.ubc\.ca/2023/04/04/ubc\-not\-enabling\-turnitins\-ai\-detection/](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/04/04/ubc-not-enabling-turnitins-ai-detection/) \(retrieved July 30\[th\] 2024\)

\[3\] “UBC affirms decision to not enable Turnitin’s AI detection feature” August 2023 [https://lthub\.ubc\.ca/2023/08/28/ubc\-affirms\-decision\-to\-not\-enable\-turnitin\-ai\-detection/](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/08/28/ubc-affirms-decision-to-not-enable-turnitin-ai-detection/) \(retrieved July 20\[th\] 2024\)

\[4\] Weber\-Wulff, D\., Anohina\-Naumeca, A\., Bjelobaba, S\. *et al\.* Testing of detection tools for AI\-generated text\. *Int J Educ Integr* **19**, 26 \(2023\)\. [https://doi\.org/10\.1007/s40979\-023\-00146\-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-023-00146-z)

---

#### *Resources*

-   [UBC Guidance on Generative AI](https://genai.ubc.ca/guidance/) includes UBC’s principles, teaching and learning guidelines, and academic integrity guidelines\.
-   [Revised Generative AI FAQ](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/chatgpt-faq/) contains information for instructors and students about how to use generative AI tools with integrity\.
-   [AI in Teaching and Learning](https://ai.ctlt.ubc.ca/) supports educators with resources from the Centre for Teaching, Learning, and Technology \(CTLT\) at UBC Vancouver, and the Centre for Teaching and Learning \(CTL\) at UBC Okanagan\.

---

#### ***Upcoming Event*s**

## **Academic Integrity Week, October 15–18**

UBC will celebrate Academic Integrity Week from October 15\-18, 2024\. Both campuses are offering events that raise awareness and encourage conversation about academic integrity\. This week will also celebrate students in their efforts to learn with integrity in their academic work\.

More information about the week’s events, and registration links, can be found on our [Academic Integrity Week page](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/academic-integrity-week/)\.

**Generative Artificial Intelligence**

# GenAI tools in teaching and learning\.

UBC is taking a measured and balanced approach to the use of genAI tools in teaching and learning, as these tools present both opportunities and risks\. GenAI tools can have the potential to enrich learning, for example by supporting idea generation, studying, or writing  – with proper acknowledgement\. Such tools can also, however, be used in ways that are detrimental to skills development, and some uses may be considered academic misconduct\. It is also important to pay attention to other risks and ethical considerations, including copyright and intellectual property, accessibility, bias, and harmful outputs, to name a few\.

Individual faculty members and program leads are the subject experts best placed to be able to determine if and how such tools are integrated into the curriculum, and it is important to clearly communicate these decisions and their rationale to students\. UBC has developed guidance to support ethical, intentional, and acknowledged use of GenAI in various areas, including teaching and learning\.

## Generative AI FAQ

Generative Artificial Intelligence \(GenAI\) tools are changing the way we teach, learn and work at UBC\. This list brings together important questions, answers, and considerations about generative artificial intelligence in the classroom for instructors and students at UBC\.  If you have an academic integrity related GenAI question that is not answered here, we invite you to share it through the website [feedback form](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/contact/)\.    

### Is the use of AI tools considered to be academic misconduct at UBC?  

The use of ChatGPT or other generative AI tools does not automatically equate to academic misconduct at UBC\. At this time, whether the use of AI tools in courses is or is not allowed is a course or program\-level decision\. Individual instructors should clarify expectations with their students early in the term, such as on the syllabus\. If instructors have questions about any Department or~~f~~ program level policies on artificial intelligence tools, they should reach out to their Department or program\. Further information is available on [generative AI syllabus language](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/generative-ai-syllabus/)\.  

-   If using ChatGPT and/or generative AI tools on coursework has been **prohibited** by the instructor, then using these tools to complete assignments would be considered  academic misconduct\.   
-   If using ChatGPT and/or generative AI tools has been **permitted** by the instructor, then instructors should make sure to convey the limitations of use and how it should be acknowledged and use should stay within those bounds\.    
-   If the use of ChatGPT and/or generative AI tools has **not been discussed or specified** by the instructor, then it could be considered as prohibited as an example of the “use or facilitation of unauthorized means to complete an examination or coursework” and more specifically as “accessing websites or other online resources not specifically permitted by the instructor or examiner” \(Discipline for Academic Misconduct, [**Vancouver**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,0) and [**Okanagan**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1547) 3\.1\.b\.iv\), and potentially plagiarism \(3\.1\.e\)\. Students should discuss this with their instructor if it is not addressed on the syllabus\. 

Students should not assume that all available technologies are permitted\. If students are not sure about whether AI tools are allowed, as with any tool, they must ask their instructor for clarity and guidance\.       

UBC’s Academic Calendar provides guidance on what is considered academic misconduct \(Academic Misconduct by UBC Students, [**Vancouver**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1745) and [**Okanagan**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1547)\)\. Academic misconduct is any conduct by which a student gains or attempts to gain an unfair academic advantage or benefit, thereby compromising the integrity of the academic process\. Artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT are not expressly named in the academic misconduct regulation but their use could be considered an attempt to gain an unfair academic advantage, as well constituting unauthorized means to complete an assignment or assessment, the accessing of a website that is not permitted, or other, depending on the specific case\.     

It is important for instructors to address academic integrity throughout the semester\. Create opportunities to discuss expectations around academic integrity ahead of assignments and exams and throughout the term\. Refer to [**academicintegrity\.ubc\.ca**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/) for [**tools to teach academic integrity and respond to academic misconduct\.**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/faculty-start/)   
 

### Can students use AI tools in their courses?  

Students may use GenAI in work submitted for courses or other academic requirements only if expressly permitted within their courses or programs\. They may choose to use GenAI to support their learning in other ways, within the bounds of legal and university policies and requirements, and the guidelines below\.   

Students should discuss this with their instructor if it is not addressed on the syllabus\.  
 

### Can or should instructors use AI detectors to detect the use of AI tools on assignments or assessments? 

The use of applications to detect AI\-generated content is strongly discouraged at this time, due to concerns about effectiveness, accuracy, bias, privacy, and intellectual property\.      
   
Despite a number of AI writing detectors being available, recent research has found that all fail to perform accurately enough, and accuracy is further reduced when simple obfuscation techniques are used\.

If instructors still choose to use AI detectors, they should be aware and understand their limitations and issues they can raise\. None of the detectors has undergone a UBC Privacy Impact Assessment, and as such there may be privacy and security concerns with submitting student work to them, particularly without student knowledge or consent\. Instructors should not use these tools to evaluate any student work that contains the name of the student or any other personal information of the student or third parties\. If student work may be submitted through one or more AI detectors, instructors should be transparent with students and let them know at the beginning of the term, such as in the syllabus\.   

Finally, it is recommended that AI detection tools not be used as the sole factor in decision\-making around an allegation of academic misconduct\. If an instructor suspects that an assignment or assessment has been completed with unauthorized use of AI tools, they should proceed as they would for any other potential allegation of academic misconduct\. An [overview of the academic misconduct process for instructors](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/faculty/) is available on the academic integrity website\. 

### Can I use Turnitin’s new AI\-detection feature in my courses? 

No, currently Turnitin’s new AI\-detection functionality is not available for use in any UBC course\. [**UBC has reaffirmed their decision to not enable Turnitin’s new AI\-detection feature**](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/08/28/ubc-affirms-decision-to-not-enable-turnitin-ai-detection/)\. 

On April 4 2023, Turnitin activated [**a new and separate feature**](https://www.turnitin.com/solutions/ai-writing) that attempts to identify AI\-generated text \. The LT Hub Leadership group, with the support of the Provosts at both UBC Vancouver and UBC Okanagan, made the decision not to enable this feature at that time \([April 2023](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/04/04/ubc-not-enabling-turnitins-ai-detection/)\) and has recently reaffirmed their decision \([August 2023](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/08/28/ubc-affirms-decision-to-not-enable-turnitins-ai-detection/)\) for the following reasons:    
 

**Effectiveness of the feature is still unclear**  

-   Testing for accuracy in the AI\-detection feature is in early stages\. 
-   Testing for potential bias in the feature continues to be in early stages\. 
-   Ability of the feature to keep up with rapidly evolving AI is unknown\. 

  
**It is not possible to double\-check or review the results**  

-   Instructors cannot double\-check the feature results\.  
-   Results from the feature are not available for students to review\.  

You can read more about UBC’s [**decision to not enable Turnitin’s new AI\-detection**](https://lthub.ubc.ca/2023/08/28/ubc-affirms-decision-to-not-enable-turnitins-ai-detection/) feature on UBC’s Learning Technology Hub website\.  

UBC is continuing to wait before deploying any AI\-detection features, including the one by Turnitin, as more information is needed about the feature’s effectiveness, accuracy and bias mitigation, and about the ability to employ an AI detector as a robust component of talking to students about suspected academic misconduct\. The use of other AI detection tools is also not recommended, due to similar issues as those noted above, as well as privacy and security concerns; to date, no AI detection tool has undergone a UBC Privacy Impact Assessment process\.   

### What should I do if I suspect the unauthorized use of AI tools? 

Instructors who suspect that a student has used generative artificial intelligence tools contrary to expectations should follow the [standard academic misconduct process](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/faculty/)\.  If an instructor has a suspicion based on the student’s work, they should follow the procedure as they would for any misconduct allegation\. Instructors should not rely on AI detectors to form the basis of an allegation of academic misconduct \.

If students have concerns about any allegations of academic misconduct against them, they can reach out to the [Office of the Ombudsperson for Students](https://ombudsoffice.ubc.ca/contact-us/), [AMS Advocacy](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-services/advocacy/) or [SUO Advocacy](https://www.suo.ca/suo-advocacy-office/)\.

### What are the recommendations for citing content developed by Generative AI if its use is permitted? 

There has been much conversation about how generative AI should be cited if its use is permitted in assignments and academic publications\. The [**American Psychological Association**](https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt) \(APA\), [**Modern Language Association**](https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai/) \(MLA\) and the [**Chicago Manual of Style**](https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/Documentation/faq0422.html) have all provided recommendations in this area\. Further information on this topic can be found in the [Generative AI and ChatGPT LibGuide](https://guides.library.ubc.ca/GenAI) from the UBC Library\. 

Updated September 11, 2024\. This Q & A was inspired by the University of Toronto’s [Chat GPT and Generative AI in the classroom](https://www.viceprovostundergrad.utoronto.ca/strategic-priorities/digital-learning/special-initiative-artificial-intelligence/) \(2023\)\.

# Academic Integrity Hub

Office of the Provost and Vice\-President, Academic

# **Supporting academic integrity awareness and education\.**

The Academic Integrity Hub is situated in the Provost’s Office at UBC Vancouver\. We promote and support a culture of academic integrity for students, instructors, and Faculties\. We develop resources, deliver workshops and events, and facilitate the diversionary process\.

**The Academic Integrity Hub works across the whole academic integrity cycle\.** We support promotion and awareness initiatives, we provide direct case management for the diversionary process, and we offer remedial education and follow up when requested\.

**The Academic Integrity Hub works with the whole UBC community\.** Our team works directly with students, instructors, Faculties and staff to support awareness around academic integrity and the academic misconduct process at UBC\.

To connect with the Academic Integrity Hub team or to learn more about our programs, please use our [contact form](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/contact/)\. 

### Our Mission

---

#### Awareness

Creating and enriching awareness of academic integrity\.

#### Education

Educating on academic integrity concepts, principles and regulations\.

#### Support

Supporting students and Faculties on the academic misconduct process\.

## Our Services

[https://academic\-integrity\-2024\.sites\.olt\.ubc\.ca/take\-five/](https://academic-integrity-2024.sites.olt.ubc.ca/take-five/)[Image](https://academic-integrity-2024.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/06/ai-hub-programs-take-5-2.jpg)

### **We facilitate the diversionary process**\.

Faculties and students work with the Academic Integrity Hub to resolve certain cases of academic misconduct\.

[LEARN MORE](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/aihub/#dp)

[Image](https://academic-integrity-2024.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2024/06/ai-hub-programs-office-hours-2.jpg)

### **We have online learning modules available\.**

Students, staff, and instructors can access several online learning courses available through Canvas\.

[LEARN MORE](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/modules)

## Diversionary Process

The diversionary process is available when a student admits to having committed academic misconduct, they do not have a previous academic misconduct record and the Dean’s Office determines that the diversionary option is appropriate\. This option consists of developing an Integrity Plan to respond to the academic misconduct with outcomes agreed upon by student and Faculty\.

The Academic Integrity Hub’s role is to facilitate and support awareness of the diversionary process\. We do not have decision\-making power around outcomes included in the Integrity Plans or other matters and are acting as a process support and information resource\.

The student has the right to provide feedback to the Faculty and not sign the plan if they have concerns or if they disagree\. Other options are available such as a Warning Letter or a referral to the President’s Advisory Committee on Student Discipline \(PACSD\)\.   
  
As of October 1, 2025, if a transcript notation of academic misconduct is agreed upon in the Diversionary Process as part of an Integrity Plan, it will appear as “**Academic Integrity Education: Integrity Plan \(Implementation Date\)**”, will remain on the transcript for one year from the date of implementation, and will be automatically removed\.

*The diversionary process pilot for UBC Vancouver commenced in Winter Session 2022/2023, Term 1\. It is currently applicable to eligible cases committed in courses offered by all Faculties\. It is also applicable to academic misconduct cases involving any academic activity undertaken while enrolled in a graduate degree program administered by the Faculty of Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies\.*

### Referral from Faculty

The Academic Integrity Hub receives referrals from the Faculty when the Dean’s Office determines that the case of academic misconduct can be suitably resolved by the diversionary process, and the student is eligible \(no previous record of academic misconduct and admitted to the misconduct\)\. The referral includes the proposed Integrity Plan\.

### Meeting with the student

Following the referral, the Academic Integrity Hub organizes a meeting with the student\. The Academic Integrity Hub presents the diversionary process to the student, answers any questions they may have, and reviews the terms of the Integrity Plan proposed by the Faculty\. As Integrity Plans are intended to be educative, the student may consider what would help them to better their understanding of academic integrity concepts or related skills\.

### Facilitation of the Integrity Plan

The Academic Integrity Hub facilitates the Integrity Plan, acting as the intermediary between Faculty and student\. This includes sharing the outcomes determined by the Faculty, having a discussion around outcomes with the student, and encouraging students to connect with other advisors and supports as needed\. The Academic Integrity Hub facilitates the signature of the Integrity Plan\.

### Follow\-up

The Academic Integrity Hub tracks completion of the outcomes of the Integrity Plans\. The Hub liaises with the Faculties and PACSD to confirm completion or to signal if students have not satisfied the terms of the agreement within the deadline\. As part of the follow\-up, students engage in an reflective and educative meeting with the Hub\.

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2022/12/dp-flowchart-vancouver-4.png)

#### Things to Remember

**Participation in the diversionary process is voluntary\.** 

An Integrity Plan is a mutual and voluntary agreement between the student and the Faculty\. Students have the right to decline a proposed Integrity Plan\. 

**The diversionary process is only available for select cases\.** 

Students will have the option to participate in the diversionary process if they have admitted to the misconduct, have no prior record of academic misconduct, and the Dean’s Office has chosen the diversionary process as the appropriate mechanism for resolution\. Access to the process is not initiated by the student or the instructor\. 

**The Academic Integrity Hub will guide and support students through the diversionary process\.** 

The Hub staff will explain the process, answer questions and concerns, and connect students with additional support\. They do not represent or advocate for the Faculty or the student\. 

### **Resources**

# ****Academic Misconduct Regulation****

Information about expectations of academic integrity and the process to follow for an allegation of academic misconduct are outlined in “Discipline for Academic Misconduct” in the Academic Calendars \([Vancouver](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,0) and [Okanagan](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,0)\)\.

## **Important links**

---

[Discipline for Academic Misconduct, Academic Calendar \(Vancouver\)](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,0)

[Discipline for Academic Misconduct, Academic Calendar \(Okanagan\)](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,0)

[PACSD Information](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/homepage/guides-and-resources/discipline/academic-misconduct/)

[Student Discipline Case Summaries](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/homepage/guides-and-resources/discipline/annual-summaries/)

[Faculty Contacts](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation/faculty-contacts/)

[Ombuds Academic Misconduct Toolkits](https://ombudsoffice.ubc.ca/our-toolkits/academic-misconduct/)

---

## Academic Misconduct Review Process

[https://academicintegrity\.ubc\.ca/regulation\-process/students/](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students/)[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2022/08/student-process.jpg)

### For Students

Academic misconduct allegations can be stressful\. Take some time to learn about your options, the process, and where to find support\.

[Information for students](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students/)

[https://academicintegrity\.ubc\.ca/regulation\-process/faculty/](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/faculty/)[instructor leaning over desk talking to students](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2021/12/ai-card-rp-faculty.jpg)

### For Faculty

Faculty members play an important role during the academic misconduct process\. This includes preventing, identifying, reviewing, and reporting academic misconduct\. 

[Information for faculty](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/faculty/)

[https://academicintegrity\.ubc\.ca/academic\-misconduct](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/academic-misconduct)[looking down towards students sitting at table working on laptops and notebooks](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2021/12/ai-card-rp-faq.jpg)

### Understanding Academic Misconduct

Some academic misconduct is obvious, and other forms are less obvious\. Make sure you know what you need to know\.

[Academic misconduct](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/academic-misconduct/)

---

## Key Terms

**Warning letter**

A Warning Letter may be issued by a Dean’s Office to a student as a response to an allegation of academic misconduct\. A Warning Letter may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Discipline for Academic Misconduct, 5\.6; [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)\.

**Diversionary Process**

The [**Diversionary Process**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/diversionary-process/) is a pathway available to Dean’s Offices to respond to academic misconduct when a student has admitted to the misconduct allegation and has no previous record of academic misconduct at UBC*\.* It is designed to be a flexible and educational process that allows Faculties to tailor responses to misconduct through a voluntary agreement with the student \(an “Integrity Plan”\) \(Discipline for Academic Misconduct, 6; [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option)\)\.

**Integrity Plan**

An Integrity Plan is a voluntary agreement between student and Dean’s Office that includes a description of the academic misconduct incident and agreed\-upon outcomes to respond to the academic misconduct\. Examples of outcomes that may be included in an Integrity Plan are listed in the Academic Calendars \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option)\)\. An Integrity Plan is part of a student’s record of academic misconduct and may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Discipline for Academic Misconduct, 5\.6; [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)\.

**PACSD**

The **President’s Advisory Committee on Student Discipline \(sometimes referred to as the “President’s Committee”\)** advises the President on matters of academic discipline through a formal hearing process \(Academic Calendar: [**Vancouver**](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee) and [**Okanagan**](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee)\)\. The PACSD has a committee for each UBC campus\. Allegations of academic misconduct referred to the PACSD that have yet to be determined, and findings of academic misconduct by the PACSD and the President’s decision letter as to the appropriate discipline \(if any\) may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Discipline for Academic Misconduct, 5\.6; [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)\.

*This is an educative website intended to support understanding of the topics and associated processes and does not constitute legal advice nor impose legal obligations on the University\. The content of this site may be updated\. The Academic Calendar is the official governing document, and where there is any inconsistency or contradiction between this educative website and the Academic Calendar provisions governing academic integrity and academic misconduct, the Academic Calendar governs\.*

# **Understanding Academic Misconduct**

Every student at UBC is responsible for informing themselves about UBC’s standards of academic integrity\. If a student is ever in doubt about expectations of academic integrity or what “counts” as academic misconduct, they must ask their instructor for clarification as soon as possible, and should not submit work for evaluation if unclear as to the relevant standard of academic integrity\. Instructors should familiarize themselves with what constitutes academic misconduct at UBC to help students avoid issues and be able to detect problems when they arise\.

UBC’s expectations of academic integrity can be found in the Academic Calendar \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/1-expectations-academic-integrity) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/1-expectations-academic-integrity)\)\.

## Important Links

---

[Academic misconduct regulation](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process)

[Academic misconduct process: Information for students](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students)

[Academic misconduct process: Information for faculty](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/faculty)

If you are suspected of academic misconduct, learn more about the [misconduct process](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students/) and available [supports](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/resources/)\.

---

## What is Academic Misconduct?

Academic misconduct includes certain prohibited conduct, including any conduct by which a student gains or attempts to gain an unfair academic advantage or benefit thereby compromising the integrity of the academic process, or helping or attempting to help another person commit an act of academic misconduct or gain, or attempt to gain, an unfair academic advantage\.

Academic misconduct can take many forms\. The Academic Calendars \(**[Vancouver](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1745)** and **[Okanagan](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1547)**\) provide examples of different forms of academic misconduct, and it is important that everyone understands these\. Note that these examples are not an exhaustive list, and there may be other behaviours that meet the definition of academic misconduct\.

## Submitting false or incomplete information

Providing false or incomplete records or information to UBC, or failing to provide relevant information when requested, can be considered a form of academic misconduct\. Students are expected to provide true and complete information in their academic work and in any applications to UBC programs, including requests for academic concessions\. 

Some examples of submitting false information may include: 

-   Lying to an instructor about being sick or providing a falsified doctor’s note to miss an exam or receive an extension
-   Falsifying grades on co\-op applications
-   Misrepresenting academic credentials to gain admission to a UBC program

## Cheating

Cheating includes a wide variety of behaviours where students gain \(or attempt to gain\) an unfair academic advantage in their academic work\. It generally involves using or facilitating an unauthorized means to complete an examination or coursework\.

Some examples of cheating may include:

-   Falsifying any part of an academic assessment
    -   Tampering with or misrepresenting research data\.
    -   Changing answers on a previously graded exam and submitting for a regrade\.
-   Participating in unauthorized collaboration
    -   Using answers or receiving assistance from others on an individual assignment\.
-   Using or facilitating an unauthorized means to complete an examination or coursework
    -   Using an unauthorized resource \(“cheat”\) sheet or electronic device during a test or exam\.
    -   Using GenAI tools to help you complete your assignment without permission\.
    -   Looking at someone else’s answers during a test or exam, with or without their knowledge\.
    -   Using another person or commercial service \(with or without payment\) to complete your academic work \(“[contract cheating](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/teaching-and-learning/contract-cheating/)”\)\.

## Failure to follow examination rules or policies

It is important to follow any rules or directions given to you by an instructor or examiner, or any other policy relating to examinations\. This includes only bringing materials or devices to the exam that have been specifically permitted by your instructor or examiner\. 

These rules are in place to help make sure examinations are fair and secure\. Failure to follow them may be considered academic misconduct\.

Some examples of exam policy violations may include:

-   Speaking to others during the exam
-   Looking at your neighbour’s answers
-   Exposing your exam materials to other students
-   Using or being in possession of any material, device or resource other than those authorized by the examiner\(s\)
-   Taking examination material out of the exam room without permission
-   Taking photos of the exam without permission

Be sure to familiarize yourself with the *Student Conduct During Examinations* policy \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/academic-assessment/student-conduct-during-examinations) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/academic-assessment/examinations/student-conduct-during-examinations)\)\.

## Plagiarism

Plagiarism means presenting someone else’s ideas and work as your own without giving them proper credit\. Scholarship involves examining and referring to the thoughts and writings of other people\. It is critical to properly cite and acknowledge whenever you are using another person’s words, ideas, or work\. 

Some examples of plagiarism may include:

-   Copy and pasting a quote or passage from a source into your essay without citing the original author\.
-   Rewriting an excerpt or passage into your own words \(“paraphrasing”\) without acknowledging the original source\.
-   Partially rewriting a passage and citing the source but relying too heavily on the language and structure of the original work, so that the result is overly similar \(“patchwriting”\)\.
-   Submitting draft work without proper referencing\.

If you need guidance on how to properly cite others’ work, the [**UBC Library**](https://guides.library.ubc.ca/apacitationstyle) has guides to help you out\. You might also wish to meet with a UBC writing consultant **\(**[**Vancouver**](https://writing.library.ubc.ca/?login) and [**Okanagan**](https://students.ok.ubc.ca/academic-success/learning-hub/writing-language/)**\)**, or explore our [**self\-guided Canvas courses**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/modules/) about writing and plagiarism\. 

## Self\-Plagiarism

Self\-plagiarism involves reusing your previous academic work, whether in whole or parts of it, without appropriate referencing and without authorization from your instructor\. Self\-plagiarism is also known as dove\-tailing or double\-dipping\. 

This form of academic misconduct often catches many students by surprise\. If you did the work, shouldn’t you be able to use it for more than one class? The answer is no, not unless you have special permission from your instructor *and* you cite yourself\. Once you have submitted your work the first time, it is no longer considered new and original work\. Reusing it without permission and acknowledgement can be considered self\-plagiarism, which is a form of academic misconduct\.

Some examples of self\-plagiarism may include:

-   Resubmitting an essay used for credit in a previous course\.
-   Reusing part of a previous assignment for credit in another course\.
-   Making minor changes to a previous assignment and submitting it for credit in another course\.

## Impersonation

Pretending that you are someone else in order to do the work of another student, or allowing someone else to impersonate you during an exam or any other academic assessment, is a very serious form of academic misconduct\.

Some examples of impersonation may include:

-   Sharing your campus\-wide login information with someone else so that they can complete and submit your assignments\.
-   Having someone else record your oral language exam on your behalf\.
-   Falsely identifying yourself as another student during an examination\.

*This is an educative website intended to support understanding of the topics and associated processes and does not constitute legal advice nor impose legal obligations on the University\. The content of this site may be updated\. The Academic Calendar is the official governing document, and where there is any inconsistency or contradiction between this educative website and the Academic Calendar provisions governing academic integrity and academic misconduct, the Academic Calendar governs\.*

# ****Academic Misconduct Process: Information** **for Students****

Facing an allegation of academic misconduct can be stressful for students\. Learning about the [**academic misconduct process**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/regulation-process/students/#am-process-student) and identifying helpful resources is an important step\.

Students do not have to go through the process alone, and [**support is available**](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/resources)\. Students can access support from the [**AMS Advocacy Office**](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-services/advocacy/), the [**GSS Advocacy Office**](https://gss.ubc.ca/advocacy/), and the [**SUO Advocacy Office**](https://www.suo.ca/suo-advocacy-office/)\. Student checklists about what to expect from the misconduct process are [**available from the Office of the Ombudsperson for Students**](https://ombudsoffice.ubc.ca/our-toolkits/academic-misconduct/)\.

The usual academic misconduct process is outlined in the Academic Calendar, *Discipline for Academic Misconduct* [\(Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct)\)\. The overall process can vary depending on the circumstances and each Faculty’s procedures, but the usual, general steps are provided below\.

## Key points for students

---

### Know your options

All misconduct cases are unique, and possible outcomes can vary case by case\.

### Know the process

It is important to inform yourself and understand the different stages of the process\. 

### Know where to get support

If you need help navigating the process or believe you have been treated unfairly, support is available\.

---

## **Academic Misconduct Process Overview**

### 1\. Allegation of academic misconduct

The academic misconduct process begins with an allegation of academic misconduct made against a student\. The allegation will go through various stages of review before the allegation is resolved by a Faculty’s Dean’s Office or the President’s Committee\.  

*Academic Calendar:* [*Vancouver*](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/4-review-allegations-faculty-members-and-deans) *and* [*Okanagan*](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/4-review-allegations-faculty-members-and-deans) 

### 2\. Instructor review and meeting

In most cases, the instructor is the first to review the facts of the allegation\. Students will usually have an opportunity to discuss the alleged misconduct with their instructor at this stage\.

All students are encouraged to be honest and forthright when faced with an allegation of academic misconduct, and to remind themselves of UBC’s expectations for academic integrity\.

Students can prepare for this conversation by informing themselves of the academic misconduct process \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct)\), reviewing material on this website, and by getting support from student advocates, the University Ombudsperson for Students, advisors, a family member, or somebody they trust\. Students usually may bring a support person to their meeting with the instructor but are expected to meet within a reasonable period of time and, if a support person attends, the student is to speak for themselves \(the support person is not the student’s representative at that meeting\)\. Students may wish to check with their Faculty about whether they need to notify their instructor in advance or provide other details\.

If after their review, the instructor concludes that misconduct has occurred, they must report the allegations in accordance with Faculty procedures\. Some Faculty procedures might involve a review of the allegation at the department or program level\. The instructor may also choose to re\-evaluate the academic merit of the work at issue\.

*Academic Calendar:* [*Vancouver*](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/4-review-allegations-faculty-members-and-deans) *and* [*Okanagan*](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/4-review-allegations-faculty-members-and-deans)

### 3\. Dean’s Office review

The Dean’s Office in the relevant Faculty reviews the allegation and may gather additional information\. Sometimes, this might involve an invitation to discuss the allegation with the Dean’s Office by meeting or email\.

If the student has not yet been given an opportunity to respond to the allegation and discuss any extenuating circumstances relevant to the alleged misconduct with their instructor, this opportunity will be provided by the Dean’s Office\.

*Academic Calendar:* [*Vancouver*](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean) *and* [*Okanagan*](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean) 

### 4\. Outcomes

After their review, the Dean’s Office chooses an appropriate pathway to resolve the allegation of academic misconduct\.

If the Dean’s Office concludes the student did not engage in misconduct, the matter is closed\. 

If the Dean’s Office concludes the student did engage in academic misconduct, there are three possible ways to resolve the misconduct:

*Academic Calendar:* [*Vancouver*](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean) *and* [*Okanagan*](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean)

### Warning Letter

The Dean’s Office issues a written reprimand to the student\. Warning Letters may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)

### Diversionary Process \(Integrity Plan\)

If a student has admitted to the academic misconduct and has no previous record of academic misconduct at UBC, and the Dean’s Office determines this option is appropriate, the Dean’s Office may propose to resolve the matter through the Diversionary Process and an Integrity Plan\. 

An Integrity Plan is a voluntary agreement between student and Dean’s Office that includes a description of the incident and agreed\-upon outcomes to respond to the misconduct\. Students have the right to decline a proposed Integrity Plan\.

Examples of Integrity Plan outcomes include, but are not limited to, re\-doing the work, a reduced grade in the course, attendance at a workshop or program for academic integrity, an apology, and transcript notation \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option#:~:text=to%20verify%20compliance.-,6.5,-The%20factors%20the) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option#:~:text=to%20verify%20compliance.-,6.5,-The%20factors%20the)\)\.

Integrity Plans are part of a student’s academic misconduct record at UBC and may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)\. 

Learn more about the Diversionary Process:

-   Campus\-specific information: UBC Vancouver and [UBC Okanagan](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/academic-integrity-ubco/)\.
-   Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) 

### PACSD

The Dean’s Office may refer an allegation to the [**President’s Advisory Committees on Student Discipline**](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/homepage/guides-and-resources/discipline/academic-misconduct/) \(PACSD\) \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee)\)\. The PACSD is the formal, impartial committee that considers allegations of misconduct against students normally through a hearing\. The PACSD communicates their findings to the President of the university, who decides on disciplinary measures \(if any\)\. 

Students will be notified via email of the time and place for the hearing\. They will also be asked to complete a [**Statement of Response**](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/sites/default/files/media-uploads/files/Statement%20of%20Response.pdf) prior to the hearing to respond to the allegations and provide relevant information and documents to the PACSD\.

Examples of disciplinary measures include, but are not limited to, zero on the assessment, failing or reduced course grade, notation of academic misconduct on student’s transcript, loss of UBC scholarships or bursaries, letter of reprimand, and a period of suspension up to and including expulsion \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/9-disciplinary-measures) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/9-disciplinary-measures)\)\.

Allegations of academic misconduct referred to the PACSD that have yet to be determined, and findings of academic misconduct by the PACSD and the President’s decision letter as to the appropriate discipline \(if any\) may impact how any subsequent incident of misconduct is responded to \(Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/5-review-allegations-dean#:~:text=of%20the%20review.-,5.6,-For%20the%20purposes)\)\.

Learn more about the PACSD process:

-   Review [Annual Summaries of Student Discipline](https://universitycounsel.ubc.ca/annual-summaries-student-discipline-cases) previously heard by the PACSD
-   Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/7-presidents-committee) 

### 5\. Student appeals of discipline

If disciplinary measures are imposed, the President will also send a copy of the Decision Letter to the applicable Senate committee for each campus that hears appeals from the President’s decision\. A student has the right to appeal the President’s decision to the applicable Senate appeal committee\. The Academic Calendars \([**Vancouver**](https://senate.ubc.ca/vancouver/rules/discipline) and [**Okanagan**](https://senate.ubc.ca/okanagan/rules/discipline/)\) outline appeals procedures\.

Academic Calendar: [Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/11-appeals) and [Okanagan](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/11-appeals)

**About academic misconduct records**

At UBC, formal discipline for academic misconduct is found in the findings of the President’s Committee \(PACSD\) and corresponding decision letter of the President\.

Generally speaking, other records relating to academic misconduct may include:

-   Warning Letters issued by a Dean’s Office;
-   Integrity Plans;
-   Allegations of academic misconduct referred to the President’s Committee that have yet to be determined;
-   Findings of the PACSD and the President’s corresponding decision letter where an allegation was found not to be substantiated; and
-   Faculty\-level records relating to allegations\.

Some, but not all, cases of academic misconduct will result in a transcript notation\. Students may receive a transcript notation of academic misconduct if it is included as a disciplinary outcome in the President’s decision letter \(“academic misconduct”\), or as an agreed\-upon outcome in an Integrity Plan \(“Academic Integrity Education: Integrity Plan \[Date\]”\)\. 

Records relating to academic misconduct are [confidential](https://privacymatters.ubc.ca/i-want/yourdata) and are retained and disclosed in accordance with the *Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act\.* 

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/09/Academic-Misconduct-Process-Flowchart-vertical-Aug2026.png)

---

**Top 10 things to know**

There are some essential things for students to know about academic integrity and academic misconduct\. 

[Top 10 things](https://academic.ubc.ca/teaching-learning/10-things-ubc-students-should-know/academic-integrity)

**Resources and support**

There are many resources available to help you learn about academic integrity, avoid misconduct, and navigate the academic misconduct process\.

[Resources for students](https://academicintegrity.ubc.ca/resources/)

# **Diversionary Process** **for** **Admitted** **Academic Misconduct**

The academic misconduct regulation includes a Diversionary Process option to resolve incidents of admitted academic misconduct through a voluntary agreement \(“Integrity Plan”\) between Dean’s Offices and students \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) and [Okanagan\)](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option)\. 

An Integrity Plan includes a description of the incident and agreed\-upon outcomes to respond to the misconduct\. Examples of outcomes that may be included in an Integrity Plan are provided in the Academic Calendar \([Vancouver](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option) and [Okanagan\)](https://okanagan.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/student-conduct-and-discipline/discipline-academic-misconduct/6-integrity-plans-diversionary-option)\.

The Diversionary Process aims to create a streamlined response for appropriate instances of admitted academic misconduct while also enriching educative approaches to academic misconduct cases\. The Diversionary Process removes or diverts these matters from being addressed by the President’s Advisory Committee on Student Discipline \(PACSD\) and potential discipline imposed by the President\. Further information is available about the implementation of the Diversionary Process at [**UBC Vancouver**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/vancouver/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1748) and [**UBC Okanagan**](https://www.calendar.ubc.ca/okanagan/index.cfm?tree=3,54,111,1550)\. 

## Key features

---

### **It’s mutual**

Students and faculty agree upon the plan of action\.

### **It’s clear**

The Integrity Plan sets out how the academic misconduct will be resolved\.

### It’s educative

The process gives students an opportunity to learn about academic integrity\.

[Image](https://sandbox-academic-integrity-2022.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/09/Academic-Misconduct-Process-Flowchart-Diversionary-Process-Cropped.png)
